BasePK: 2925639

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, it is well known that I participate frequently in what is called the "Late Night Show". Some people ask why, and the answer is that I am a great lover of crowds and there is nothing like a large and enthusiastic audience to turn me on.
A few days ago I asked a question about the measures being taken to assist the people of Prince Edward Island who suffered severe crop damage, besides loss of electricity and telephone services, as a result of a severe storm in what is well know as the garden province. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) seemed to be well briefed on the issues and I congratulate him on the lucidity, fulsomeness and directness of his reply. He might well serve as a model to other parliamentary secretaries, and indeed to those lofty incumbents of the treasury benches.
870

October 29, 1974
Adjournment Debate
A great many islanders were seriously inconvenienced for a period of a week and, in some cases, for a little longer. Shortages of utilities, water, light and fuel made life difficult for the people and for their farm animals. There was a threat to our valuable potato crop and to such grain as was not harvested. I now hear less disturbing reports than were coming my way when I first asked the question. Yet to many people this was not an inconvenience of a minor nature. For a week it was impossible to telephone to my residence in Prince Edward Island, as I discovered daily. Many homes were unheated for days. The utility companies moved as best they could to get things back to normal.
My main concern has to do with the alacrity of the movement of aid toward provinces and regions affected by seriously adverse weather conditions. From time to time in this House I have heard members bring forward appeals arising from emergency situations in their home areas, inquiring about federal aid and being advised that no official request had yet come from the province concerned. In many cases speed is of the essence, and I would urge greater co-ordination so that there might be a diminution of the waiting period.
In July of this year a freak storm damaged crops in my constituency. Appeals for compensation were made, discussed and processed, but it was a long time before the victims of the storm were able to receive funds, or even to receive assurances as to the measure of aid which would come to them. In these days it is not easy to wait. Time is money, and during a period of inflation money is shrinking.
It is ironic I should be talking about two grim assaults from nature on Prince Edward Island-strange, because this summer was one of the most beautiful and balmy in the island's history, as many thousands of tourists can testify. I appeal for a method whereby the whole procedure for making aid available in such cases can be improved and expedited.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Agriculture and it arises from the present sizeable build-up of turkeys in storage in Canada. What does the government intend to do about managing these turkeys stocks? I ask this question because during the first part of October there were some 77 million pounds of turkeys in storage as compared with some 46 million pounds in storage in October of last year and 16 million pounds in September of last year.

BasePK: 2925858

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I was unable to conclude my remarks on this bill last night and am pleased to have this further opportunity to speak. I wonder how this bill, if passed, would stand up in court if the competition bill presented by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) becomes law. Misrepresentations have been made concerning this bill, and in the next few minutes I propose, for the benefit of producers and consumers, to reveal facts and figures which will show exactly what is taking place.
The minister suggested-this is significant-that this bill, once passed, will keep bread prices down by five cents a loaf. The consumer will benefit, according to the minister. He did not say that the Canadian producer of Red Spring wheat-that is, the producer in western Canada and, to some degree, in Ontario-is to subsidize the price of bread to the tune of three cents a loaf. The bill does not mention this fact, either. We must recognize that the western grain producer has just emerged from one of his most difficult periods in history because of low selling prices of wheat.
The recent strike of grain handlers on the west coast may not have affected very much the amount of grain used domesticallv in Canada, but it did affect the economic well-being of the grain producer. During that strike tne minister in charge of the Wheat Board, who is supposed to protect and work for the interests of producers, told western Canadian farm organizations to settle the strike with the grain handlers' union on the basis of the Perry report. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had also thrown their weight behind that report. Clearly, the minister was trying to get his colleagues off the hook. The prairie producer is to be commended for not taking the bait of the minister.
Now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) is on the hook because the government forced the producers to settle for a 61 per cent increase to the grain handlers and Treasury Board is now offering 16 per cent to the grain inspectors who work for them. These men work side by side. I wish to quote a few facts from the August 28 edition of the Montreal Star, as follows:
Put into annual terms, the conciliation board report calls for a base pay increase from $10,316 a year to $12,126 next year and to $13,478 the following year.
In addition to that, there is a cost of living index, plus a pension benefit. This runs to about $17,000 or $18,000. With regard to the income of producers, the article states:

October 30, 1974
Wheat Payments
Even in 1973, which by no stretch of the imagination can be regarded as a normal year, average net income of Alberta farmers was about $12,100; and of Saskatchewan farmers about $12,500.
In 1972, a more typical year, average net income of Alberta farmers was about $5,600; and of Saskatchewan farmers about $5,400. And the average was lower in 1971 and 1970.
The figures for the producers do not include pension benefits. The figures for the grain handlers do. Therefore, there is a vast difference. Approximately 8V4 cents worth of flour, including milling costs, goes into a 24-ounce loaf of bread. At the present time, bread sells for between 40 and 48 cents a loaf, depending on whether it is a private brand or a name brand. In the last year, direct labour cost in the production of bread increased between 17 and 18 per cent. Unless the government is prepared to bring inflation under control, this type of increase will continue year after year; there will be no end to it.
The profits of the bakeries run from zero to 1 Vi per cent. That is not a great profit. We cannot condemn the bakeries for what they are doing; they are caught up in a series of regulations which are prescribed by government officials and they are being buried under the load. They have great difficulty dealing with these regulations. The cost of packaging, which the modern housewife demands, is up 84 per cent over last year. In addition, I understand that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is demanding a list, in percentages, of all the ingredients in a loaf of bread. This adds to the cost to the consumer.
On one hand we are trying to do something for the consumer; on the other the government negates that policy by adding controls, regulations and restrictions which increase the cost to the consumer. I mentioned recently in the House that the policy of this government is causing a great deal of hardship to the business economy of Canada. This is an example. Rather than list all the ingredients of the product and their percentages, it would be far better if the government set up a nutrition information bank where information would be available for persons with allergies. There could be a data centre in Ottawa which a person could call to obtain all the details of a product. The bakeries do not criticize the policy that this information should be listed somewhere, but they recognize that it costs a lot of money to do it. This cost ultimately must be borne by the consumer under the present system.
Some consumers can afford to pay a little more for a loaf of bread. In Canada today there is a vast majority who make more money than the producer. They enjoy the benefit of the three-cent subsidy which the western producer in many cases can ill-afford. In my constituency we grow some of the best wheat in Canada. We can grow number one CW wheat most years. Land is selling in the vicinity of $500 an acre. This is not because industry is trying to buy up the land; it is foreign-controlled money which is purchasing this land. The prairie grain producer has to compete with this type of financing.
Production costs have gone up. The costs of fertilizer, machinery and labour have increased. There does not seem to be any end to the rise in the cost of production for western producers. BasePK: 2925862

Speech:
Madam Speaker, in order to speak to this bill one certainly needs to have a forked tongue, as there are in this bill principles with which one can agree, but many shortcomings which leave a great deal to be desired. When the minister introduced the bill, he suggested that it envisaged a two-price system for grain and wheat. The fact is, that is simply not the case. First of all, it does not apply to all grains, and it really does not apply to all wheats. It refers to those wheats which are sold for use and consumption in Canada. October 31, 1974
Slaughter of Calves
I am sorry that I have to say this here, but I cannot help but put myself in the position of a young, growing child in Bangladesh. It is not very hard for me to do that because I have been in such a position, I have experienced it. I daresay that there are not very many people sitting here tonight who can say the same.
This young boy in Bangladesh sees death around him every day. He watches his immediate family die. He watches his mother leave the place where they eat every day without touching the food because she wants to reserve every last particle that is available for her children. I cannot help but fear that perhaps the small boy, in this modern world of communications today, by some strange accident will read some of the press reports that have appeared in our newspapers in Canada lately. One reporter described the scene of horror in Quebec in this way:
The tiny black and white calf stumbled in a struggle to escape and its tiny hoofs slid in the blood soaking the scaffold hanging over a 30-foot-deep pit.
Roughly hauled to its feet, it grew calm, or at least motionless, as its brown eyes stared at the hundreds of carcasses below.
I could go on reading this, but my time is limited. However, it is a beautiful story. I am looking at this small boy who, by sheer accident, reads something like this, and at the same time he might be looking at the eyes of a person dying of starvation. I wonder if anybody here has ever looked into the eyes of a dying person. I have. You can see the sign in the eyes of a dying person for the whole day before his death. It is a terrible story to tell here and I know it shocks people, but obviously it is the only way in which to gain the attention of people. There are people starving to death in the world every day. There are headlines in any of the newspapers at which you would like to look. One of the articles reads as follows:
There is a severe famine throughout the country, and the most conservative estimates say 750,000 persons will likely die of starvation or diseases related to malnutrition from August through November this year.
We are living in a global community; we are talking about our immigration laws and about our responsibility to open up our borders to people from other countries, and yet we allow people in other countries to starve to death while we dump our foodstuffs.
Another thing that I have experienced, that the little boy in Bangladesh might also experience, is to have lived in a country where people were starving to death and, at the time, to have read that North America was dumping wheat into the ocean, dumping flour into the sea to maintain some kind of market stability. The press is full of stories about our rotten eggs. The global community which has access to radio and television will hear and read about those rotten eggs in Canada, about the calves we are slaughtering, and about the wheat we are dumping into the sea. I am very concerned about what this small boy might be thinking and I have an idea what it is, but I will not spatter the pages of Hansard with it. I will tell you one thing he will be thinking. If he ever gets the chance, and he likely never will, there will be an equalization of the score. However, we do not have to worry about that because he likely will never have the chance.

We have an oversupply of expensive beef and an overdemand for inexpensive beef. We must find a balance. We must consider the consequences of a great number of these small boys who say that some day they will have to equal the score. I consider it to be almost a criminal act to discourage farmers and others from producing all the food they can. The solution must obviously be for them to produce all they can.
We cannot pass laws to restrict Canadian farmers from producing the maximum. We must look at who has the responsibility of paying the bill. Certainly everyone is entitled to a profit. Everyone is entitled at least to break even. However, it has been amply demonstrated this evening that the farmer has not been breaking even. The marketer and the processor have not done too badly.
The farmer is entitled to a profit even though he is dealing in food that is hard to come by for consumers. He can be compared with the person who drives an ambulance. There was no time limit or specific time when Bill C-18 would pass out of existence.

Madam Speaker, I regret very much that there are only a few minutes left as I know there are a number of members who would like to make a contribution, some of them members on this side of the House.
I listened to the crusade for reform by the hon. member who just spoke and I could not help but remember that the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) and I represent constituencies both of which have far more people resident in them than are resident in the entire province of the hon. member which is now represented in this place by four parliamentarians and in the other place also by four. I cannot believe he was serious in suggesting that we should increase such numbers to 10. If he wants to start on reform I think he should start in his own house and look at it a little more closely.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) presented himself as having two bills, and I think the one to deal with the question of representation genuinely involves the problem of reform. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this bill is not reform and does not get to the heart of the matter.
The real problem with the other place is the lack of opposition. The opposition has dwindled to a handful, and many of them are aging and are not as forceful as they were in other years.
I listened to the hon. member who proposed this bill complain about political partisanship. I wish he had been a candidate in the election of 1962, as I was, when the Senators in the other place had a slightly different preponderance of numbers. I can remember Senator Grosart doing something somewhat similar to the job that Senator Keith Davey performed in the last election. All that time there were members on this side of the House who had some misgivings about the degree of partisanship involved.
If political partisanship is a crime then there is something wrong with our political life. Surely the very essence of our political life is a healthy interest in the democratic process. The cure lies in a better and stronger opposition in the Senate, where there should be a better balance of the parties in Canada. The real weakness of the Senate is the lack of a parliamentary opposition. That is the point to which the hon. member who moved this bill should have directed his remarks.
I listened to the arguments of the hon. member for Victoria, and at no point did he deal with the basic point of his bill; that is, limiting the length of a Senate term. This is a popular exercise and I submit that limiting the term would bring about, if it were enacted-and I do not

believe it will be enacted in this form-a discrimination against younger men in the other place. The problem of accepting a limited appointment, to those who are in a profession or business career and are younger in years, is a very serious one indeed.
We are, in my opinion, very correctly raising the question of conflict of interest. We are saying to the men and women who go to the other place they must serve full time, they must serve without conflict of interest, and they must cut their former ties. A man or woman who leaves a profession, business or usual activity, for a limited period, at the end of that period has to face the certainty of going back into civilian life, as it were, and at that point in too many cases has to start thinking of bread and butter.
In such circumstances the very quality of independence, the very quality of full-time service, and the very quality of making sure there is no conflict of interest comes, shall I say, under pressure. That is not the point. The point is that we have a Senate at this stage, whatever the faults of the system may be, and I will concede there are a number of faults. The fact is that the independence of the Senate is the very guarantee of its integrity. The amendment which is proposed in this bill does not, in my opinion, deal with it.
There are two committees about to be struck in this House; one is a joint committee of the other place and the House of Commons to deal with the Public Service of Canada, and the other will deal with the National Capital Region. We look to the other place for able and continuing representation by parliamentarians who will persist in taking an interest in these matters.
On October 30, 1972, there was a previous parliament, of which I was a member, with a number of faces that are not now here, some 120 of them. The turnover of elected representatives in the Canadian parliament is very great indeed. The other place has provided continuity on a number of committees dealing with a number of important matters.
I should like at this stage, with the indulgence of the House and if I have time, to tell a short anecdote. I regret that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) is not here. I am thinking of the problem of the lost statues.
When I was a member of a previous parliament the then minister of public works, now a member of the other place, called upon one or two of the local members, Jean Richard and myself, and said: "I have a problem and I would like local members to give me their very best advice. What do you do with certain statues?" One of them was a statue of former Prime Minister Meighen, and it was simply outrageous. It was not done by any Liberal artist; it was no Grit plot and there was no attempt at concealment, but what you would do with such a statue is utterly beyond my comprehension.

Let us look at the history of crude oil pricing in Canada, which goes back a long way. However, I will not go all the way back; I will go back only to January 7, 1973, when there was an exchange of correspondence between Mr. Getty, minister of intergovernmental affairs of the Alberta government, and the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in which the latter pledged that there would be the fullest consultation before the federal government would implement a system of crude oil export controls. One month later, with no consultation, with not so much as a "by your leave," the federal government unilaterally imposed export crude oil controls. That was the first warning, in recent times at least, that the government of Alberta in future had better get more iron-clad guarantees rather than just a letter, even though it was signed by the minister.
Then there was the energy policy that was brought down in July of 1973, and again I commend the officials of the minister's department for putting together an excellent document containing excellent advice. I think on page 9 of that document it is stated that no national oil policy can be contemplated without the fullest intergovernmental co-operation and discussion. It also said, I believe on page 14 of the document, that it did not appear practical to build a pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal to carry western crude to Montreal. On September 4, just two months later, without any consultation at all, the government introduced a new national oil policy freezing the price of western crude at $4 a barrel and committing the government to a pipeline to the Montreal market.

It is a sad history of broken promises and commitments. Small wonder that some westerners state that commitments from this minister should be obtained in writing and be witnessed. I might add that they should be bonded, as well. Not only do they freely break commitments and promises; they cannot even be counted upon to obey the law. For example, let me quote from the Mineral Transfer Act, 1930, as follows:
-the interest of the Crown in all Crown lands, mines, minerals (precious and base) and royalties derived therefrom within the province, and all sums due or payable for such lands, mines, minerals or royalties, shall, from and after the coming into force of this agreement and subject as therein otherwise provided, belong to the province-
It could not be more explicit: the royalties belong to the province. Then how is it that the Minister of Finance can introduce a budget saying that companies will treat as income for taxation purposes these royalties which the Mineral Transfer Act states belong to the province? I might add that there is another section of the BNA Act, section 125, which provides:
No lands or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation.
The hon. member for Nipissing has indicated that the federal government has jurisdiction over trade and commerce. There is no argument about that. But it is also very clear that natural resources belong to the province; and there should not be any argument about that. To what extent can one level of government, in exercising its rights under the law, impinge on the rights of another level of government? Surely common sense would indicate that the proposals contained in this legislation and those which have been put forward by the government totally contradict the law in respect of the provinces having the right of ownership over these natural resources.
Does ownership simply mean that one has title, but none of the privileges? Is an owner prevented from utilizing the lands or minerals that he owns to his own best benefit? If that is the case, what is the use of ownership if in fact some other authority, in exercising what it considers its legal right, can restrict you from exercising any of the normal prerogatives of ownership? If that were the case,

ownership would be meaningless. Surely we have not come to that in this country.
In total, the performance of this minister, of his colleague the Minister of Finance, and of the Prime Minister in respect of our oil position, has been incredibly inept and basically dishonest. Small wonder that one hears so much talk in western Canada of alienation and separation. I do not want to dwell on the subject, but it would be a great tragedy if in their arrogance the members of this government, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Minister of Finance, underestimated the depth of feeling that exists. I and all my colleagues here and in the provincial government of Alberta are Canadians first and foremost.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is similar to the one I moved a few years ago, but, in fact, his goes further. Mine only suggested that there be at least one member of parliament on the board of directors of every Crown Corporation, to ensure a better control of the expenditures the government makes through its corporations. The hon. member for Lotbiniere thinks that it might be convenient to form a special committee of the House to study every aspect of Crown corporations. It is a good suggestion, although I do not necessarily agree with
November 4, 1974

everything the hon. member said. It seems to me that this question should have been discussed long ago.

When I say I do not agree with everything the hon. member for Lotbiniere has said, what I mean is I think he has decreased his chances of having this motion passed by the House. It is not that I disagree with anything specifically in his motion, as I think it is an excellent motion, but the fact that he says we must have a special committee look into the aspects of each and every Crown corporation-at least that is the way I interpret it-means that we would have a committee studying all of these Crown corporations for a very long time. I do not know how many there are, but I think there are over 40. Therefore, for the simple reason of practicality I could not go along completely with the motion of the hon. member.
If the hon. member were to propose his motion in a different way so the House could consider asking for the subject matter to be referred to the committee I think his motion would be more acceptable to the House, and I would encourage him to do so. This is a subject that has been very dear to my heart since I have been a member, and I have spoken about it over the years.
I feel very strongly that as members of parliament we come here to represent the people of Canada and yet are unable to represent them properly simply because we have no control over certain aspects of government spending. It is suggested that Crown corporations must be autonomous and independent. We can all realize why, under certain conditions, a Crown corporation must be autonomous, but there certainly must be some kind of control, some kind of answerability, whereby Crown corporations must exercise responsibility to the people of Canada through their elected members who speak on their behalf.
Many times in this House and in committee we have asked a minister for some information, or have made a suggestion concerning a Crown corporation under his aegis, and have been told that that body is autonomous, is independent, and therefore he will have to refer the matter to that corporation.
In many instances the minister seems to have absolutely no control over such bodies. We could take almost any Crown corporation as an example. The CNR is an obvious one. The CBC is another. No one wants to control the press of this country. I am sure no one would suggest that the government should control the CBC. On the one hand while no one suggests the government should have control over the press, on the other hand such a body as the CBC should not have licence-which very often is the term used in the name of freedom of the press-to do whatever it wishes. There must be certain norms established, and I say this must come through the voices of the representatives of the people.
I wonder whether perhaps the hon. member would consider making an appeal to the government on the basis that it really is not necessary to have Crown corporations examined in detail by a committee but rather that we should have an opportunity in committee to examine all the general aspects of Crown corporations, and particularly the answerability feature.
Crown Corporations
In the past I have suggested that members of parliament should be members of the boards of directors of Crown corporations. This has been done in some provinces. It has also been done in some other countries. However, this has not met with complete approval in this House up until now. Perhaps this is not the answer, but at least it is a suggestion. It would seem to me that a special committee, such as the committee proposed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), could be the vehicle to examine the feasibility and the pros and cons in respect of members of parliament being on those boards. The committee could examine all the other aspects having to do with the answerability of these corporations to the people of Canada through their representatives. So I would make that suggestion to the hon. member. Perhaps he might see his way clear to do this.
I rather think the government would be of a mind to accept that kind of approach. From what I understand- and I hope this is the case-more and more items discussed here in private members' hour, whether by way of notices of motions or specific bills, will be referred to committees, or at least their subject matters will be so referred. This does not necessarily mean that the government says it will grab the ideas proposed, but rather that it will allow such items to go to a committee for study. I believe this is a great step forward because, in the last few years, it has developed that private members' hour has been nothing but a time for members to come forward with their favourite ideas only to find that no one would listen, and that motions and bills would simply be talked out. It certainly is not my desire to talk out this particular motion. I simply want to say I would encourage the hon. member to use this approach to the government, and I would encourage the spokesman for the government to recommend that this matter be referred to a committee so that the general aspect can be studied in detail.

The question is: to what extent are we as a people, as individuals, as a nation, prepared to move away from our own self-centredness and start thinking of others?
I was interested listening to the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). I always enjoy his contributions, and I would like to reply to some of the things he said in the serious way in which everyone is discussing these serious problems today. On the question of government priorities the hon. member pointed out, and it is true, that government has all kinds of priorities in the same way that people have all kinds of priorities. There is inflation that they are worried about; there are priorities with regard to employment. But how do those priorities really compare with the priorities being faced by millions of people in the world who are nearing starvation?

In our society we have become accustomed to taking each other apart about things which, at best, are merely increments to our already high standard or living. When you place the problems we face against those faced by much of the rest of the world, certainly our difficulties pale by comparison. Can there really be any question of juggling priorities when so much of the world is facing death from starvation? Is it not time we realized that there is one central priority-our responsibility to other human beings? The great failure of modern society has been its failure to find this technique. Toynbee's solution is a return to religion. But if you want to take it in a broader sense, what Toynbee is really suggesting is a return to morality. Now, for many, religion has lost its hold, but surely the basis of religion, the idea of morality, has not lost its hold and should not lose its hold on the western world.
It is true we can do all these things mentioned by Toynbee, but we have to see this as a moral issue in order to meet the challenge we face. We have to look at it from the viewpoint of all out production in order to prevent a great many of the people of the world from starving. This is the kind of approach we should now take to agriculture. This is the kind of planning we must do in our own country before suggesting that the world should also plan.
When you look at agriculture in those terms, you get an entirely different perspective. I think we have made a decent gesture at the food conference in offering one million tons of grain a year. I was approached on many occasions by ministers of agriculture from developing countries who wanted to get bilateral development aid from Canada. They were looking for Canadian agricultural technology to use in their countries because they think Canada has the best technology and the most productive agriculture in the world. They also know that they can get help from Canada without political strings attached, if they are willing to make the effort to help themselves. It is still too early to make an adequate assessment of the World Food Conference. Nonetheless, I believe that there are real reasons for being optimistic. Perhaps the most important of these is that as a result of the conference many countries will start increasing their food production earlier than they would have.
Several resolutions were passed by the plenary session of the conference. However, the accepted wording of the resolutions was made on the basis of oral amendments, and final wordings of the resolutions are not yet available. Most important among the resolutions is the one to establish a fund to be called the international fund for agricultural development. The fund would finance agricultural and fisheries development projects in developing countries. Contributions to it would be on a voluntary basis.

The fact that the resolution's co-sponsors included oil producing nations such as Iran, Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela may be regarded as a commitment by these countries to use some of their financial resources, and we hope they will, to support a multilateral program for agriculture and fisheries development.
The conference has asked the FAO and other concerned international organizations such as the International Wheat Council to make the arrangements necessary for the establishment of a global information and early warning system on food and agriculture. The objectives, policies and guidelines as set out in the text of the proposed FAO international undertaking on world food security were also endorsed by the conference. Governments of major exporting and importing nations have been invited to enter discussions on the feasibility of establishing grain reserves in appropriate locations. The Director General of the FAO has convened a meeting of representatives of interested countries for November 29 to look at the shortterm problems of the developing countries most seriously affected by current food shortages.
The arrangements for follow-up at the conference were covered in a complicated resolution that in effect sets up a world food council at the ministerial level that would report to the United Nations General Assembly through the Economic and Social Council. The World Food Council would serve to co-ordinate follow-up policies concerning food production, nutrition, food security, food trade and food aid. Membership of the World Food Council has yet to be determined, but its members will be nominated by the Economic and Social Council and elected by the United Nations General Assembly.
The conference did recommend, among other things, an FAO committee on world food security, an intergovernmental committee of the World Food Program, and that the board of directors of the international fund for agricultural development should submit periodic reports to the World Food Council. The conference also requested that international groups and organizations take leadership in following up the results of the conference. The conference did adopt a long declaration entitled "Declaration on the eradication of hunger". Its final wording is not yet available, but it is a document that contains the suggestions of many groups that were agreeable to others, and hence is perhaps weaker than we would have liked because of the need for consensus.
Canada's leadership and contribution to the conference is perhaps best summed up in a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs dated November 9, from Mr. Aquino, executive director of the World Food Program, as follows:
I would again like to express to you, and through you, also to the Secretary of State for Agriculture, the hon. We in the World Food Program are deeply appreciative of the leading role CIDA has long taken and so clearly intends to continue to take in helping to "seek the elimination of hunger". Your moving speech and very practical undertakings and proposals are certainly most encouraging.

I discuss this question as one who, throughout his political life, has been a firm advocate of a strong federal government. I would go further. The New Democratic Party has consistently supported the concept of a strong federal government clothed with the power necessary to deal effectively with social and economic problems. For instance, the New Democratic Party advocated and supported a two price system for oil, and a single price across Canada, in order to protect the Canadian people against the 400 per cent increase in international oil prices.

If this bill is passed it will provide that, in the event negotiations are not successful with the provinces, the government may establish a price in Canada for all oil and gas entering into interprovincial and international trade. On November 13 and 14 I argued in this House that the federal government must have that power if we are going to deal with the problem of energy supplies in this country. I must say, however, that the budget may cause us to re-examine our position if the federal government intends to use its powers in the ruthless manner which it is now displaying.
Canada needs a strong federal government in order to cope with the many problems of this country, and nowhere is this more necessary than in the field of energy where we are faced with a crisis in the years immediately ahead.

They agreed to accept a price of $6.50 per barrel, when the Chicago price at that time was between $10 and $11 per barrel, and now it is much higher. Every barrel of oil sold in Alberta and Saskatchewan is being sold for $5 less than could be secured on the Chicago market, plus transportation. In other words, the provinces gave up over $2 billion. I am one who supported what they did. Considering the type of national emergency we faced then and which we still face, a price must be set to protect the Canadian people from exorbitant international oil prices. The provincial premiers agreed to this.
Further, they agreed to forgo the 50 per cent share of revenue from the export tax which they had received up until then. Those were great concessions, and the Prime Minister was right in saying they were made possible only with the good will and deep commitment of the provincial governments concerned.

The March 27 meeting of the first ministers was primarily a formalization of agreements reached earlier in the month between the Prime Minister and the premiers of Saskatchewan and Alberta. This is an important point, and it is one which is made clear in the correspondence which was tabled in the House on Monday by the Prime Minister. Two points are crucial to the understanding of the substance and process of the unilateral breaking of this commitment by the federal government. First, in his two letters to premiers Blakeney and Lougheed dated March 12, the Prime Minister refers to the "one year accord" reached between him and the premiers. Second, in both these letters, in addition to the agreement on price- and contrary to what the Prime Minister said this afternoon, this was not simply an agreement on price-there was a specific commitment not to consider for equalization purposes oil revenue placed by the provinces in special capital funds to be used for the development of future energy sources. I quote from the Prime Minister's letter to Premier Blakeney, dated March 12:
I understand that it is intended that the funds shall be used to develop sources of energy to replace the diminishing oil reserves. Under such circumstances we would propose that these capital amounts would not be included in the revenue base for equalization.
Nothing could be less unambiguous. The same commitment was made in the Prime Minister's letter to Premier Lougheed. In his reply on this point, Premier Blakeney concurred and requested an assurance that-and I quote- "this approach will not be abandoned to our detriment after the interim agreement expires." What Mr. Blakeney did not know was that the federal government would not wait until the one-year period of the agreement had expired before taking action. The budget presented by the Minister of Finance last week completely reneged on this commitment. The provision which stipulates that one-third of the additional oil revenues in the oil producing provinces would be considered for equalization purposes clearly revokes the commitment made by the Prime Minister last March. The Saskatchewan government has calculated that this will cost them about $40 million.
The New Democratic Party opposes, in the strongest possible terms, this course of events. We urge the government to live up to its commitments to the oil producing provinces by withdrawing the provision that one-third of the oil revenue be considered for equalization purposes. provision for non-deductibility of provincial royalties for tax purposes as applied to corporations in the resource sector. Such steps are not only compatible with a strong and stable federal government, but under present circumstances they are essential to its realization.

BasePK: 2933554

Speech:
Yes, certainly. He was receptive to the proposal that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections be asked to review the whole question of redistribution.
On July 5, 1973 Bill C-208 was brought in to set aside the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, and the matter was referred to committee. The bill passed committee on July 12 and was given third reading in the House on July 13. I mention those dates because in just two short weeks the whole matter of setting aside redistribution was handled by the House. Seven months later the matter of seeking a new redistribution method was brought to the committee, that is, on February 29, 1974. At that time the then president of the privy council presented some alternatives to the committee, and this took up the total time of the committee on that day. Two months later, on April 9, the committee had a meeting to discuss this redistribution method recommended by the president of the privy council, and that was the only discussion that that method was given. Essentially there has been no opportunity for members of the House to indicate their reaction to the government's recommendation, no opportunity for public debate, no opportunity for the media and for observers of parliamentary processes to react to that method or discuss it.
For that reason it seems to me highly inappropriate for the government at this time to bring in a bill calling for the implementation of a method which has had no analysis or discussion and to ask for the approval of the House. It would be irresponsible for us to grant the government's request. It is especially galling, and I wonder about the priorities of the government.
A week or two ago I received a letter concerning the Abbott Commission, a commission established to look at the question of facilities and space for parliament. It is a commission with representation from both sides of the House, the Senate and outside people. It has staff and an office, it will travel to hear witnesses, and in fact will undertake an extensive study of facilities for parliament. Surely the question of redistribution, of how many members we will have in the House and what the regional representation will be, as well as how well protected will be the small provinces, is at least as important as how many offices and committee rooms we will have.

provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan voluntarily agreed last March to subsidize every consumer of oil products in this country to the extent of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a year. They did that as Canadians. They were praised in this House by all parties for their statesmanship.

I want to put something forward for the government's consideration because eventually this has to be dealt with by the government as a whole, not just by the parliamentary secretary or someone else. people east of the Ottawa Valley line, that will keep one price across Canada which is lower than the world price, that will allow for the cushioning effect of staging to the new price levels, and will also be fair to the producer provinces and give them a quid pro quo. We, as a loyal opposition, are willing to try and end this confrontation deliberately sought by a government that is only conscious of political gimmicks to achieve its end. I have made some of these proposals to the minister in private and some in public.
The proposals we want to put forward will have to be dealt with seriously by the whole cabinet because this bill is a clear indication that it is a power device by this government to continue its gambling policy that it can smash the constitution by unilateral action while playing politics with the question of prices for the oil that heats our homes and runs our automobiles. This is a very serious thing the government is doing.
I suggest to the government supporters and to the parliamentary secretary in particular, that they carry this message back loud and clear because the people of Canada are not going to stand idly by Mr. Speaker. We in this party are the founders and fathers of the federal system. This principle of consultation which we have followed over the years has worked. I was in the Diefenbaker administration. Over 50 agreements were made with the provinces in which then the federal government took the initiative, on matters which were purely in the provincial resource area. In every case we sat down as equals with the relevant provincial government and said, "This is your resource. We even moved into the field of education. Every province signed, because they were agreements reached after consultation. We went across the field. Believing in a strong federal central government, we knew it could only be strong if we worked in harmony with the provinces which had responsibilities under their part of the constitution. If the people of Canada know what the issue is, they will opt for a type of federal system that does not have this concept of confrontation that was brought in by the Pearson administration in 1963, and continued by the present administration. Let us get this straight: when we talk about conflict of interest, we have in mind the public interest, not political interest and not institutional interest. We are thinking of the public interest as it applies to someone entrusted with safeguarding that interest. This is a much broader concept than national security, for example. It is a wide-ranging concern and goes to the very root of public confidence in our system, in our institutions, in our political process and in those who are in high positions of trust. It is within that meaning of conflict of interest that we make our case. We believe any narrower meaning is inappropriate.
In accepting this broad definition, one must recognize that there is no way of eliminating all possible conflicts of interest which may and do exist. For example, how can you eliminate the possible conflict of interest involving a minister and a friend, or a member of the House and a friend? I recognize that it is not possible to eliminate all possible conflicts of interest, but I contend that the definition of what is the public interest must be as broad as I have made it, if problems are to be faced and situations met in a way which will increase public confidence. I believe Canadians will be much more ready to accept that kind of judgment-call approach if they perceive that the call and the judgment are weighed against guidelines and rules and regulations which have more substance than those proposed so far in relation to cabinet ministers. These, surely, are not adequate to increase public confidence. I will come back to that in a moment.

In defining the policies, rules and procedures which will become law, we shall keep in mind that we are dealing with two groups of people whose influence differs according to the group involved. The first group, of course, is made up of the people sitting in Parliament. This group includes members of Parliament, cabinet ministers and parliamentary secretaries, as well as the Speaker of the House and his deputies.

The other non-elected group includes career public servants, those appointed to positions in the service. Although senators are appointed, I include them for this purpose as parliamentarians. December 11, 1974

can be done by the government in drafting the bill. Otherwise there is no flexibility on either side of the House.
I might introduce three subsidiary arguments. I really base my submission before Your Honour on what I have already said, but there are three subsidiary arguments which you might like to entertain. The first is that the text of the notice of ways and means does not apply any longer. The bill has been read a second time and referred to the committee of the whole. All that the committee has before it is the bill. Amendments that are relevant may be made, provided they do not raise the rate or the incidence of the tax and thereby infringe upon the financial initiative of the Crown or imbalance ways and means.

The only bearing on the question of the ways and means procedure is the procedure which the House has developed to maintain the Crown's financial initiative. The only purpose of a ways and means motion preceding a tax bill is to preserve the initiative of the Crown to tax, to change the ways and means of the country and add a budgetary burden upon the people. It is because of this that notice of ways and means has been a procedure of this House. Second, I might say that the original point of order, raised, as it was, on second reading might have been raised too late even at that stage. My third argument is that the committee be entitled to amend the bill to match the ways and means motion, but the chairman has no authority to order that this amendment be made: his authority is defined in the committee's reference, not with reference to the ways and means motion. I am sure Your Honour, sitting where you now do, has had occasion in the last few months to observe from that elevated position much more than you did when sitting at our level. Perhaps there have been more instances of abuse of alleged privileges than was the case in the past.
Years ago, when the issue of privilege first arose, the circumstances were quite different from those that obtain today. Today, the press gallery, its members and members of the radio and television media are the window through which the world looks in on the workings, deliberations and statements of this House. I think it is imperative-I say this as the foundation of my argument-that people outside this chamber be entitled to expect that what is said in this House is, in fact, reasonably and impartially reported.
It may well be that there are issues of bias and prejudice, and members of this House may feel they are not being reported as adequately or as often as they would like. But if it becomes evident that what is being reported as having been said in this House by members is a distortion, an exaggeration or an improper interpretation because members are paying for the privilege, then obviously the public, whom members of the press gallery and ourselves serve, will become more cynical than they have been in the past in respect of what are the true statements emanating from this House. For instance, scandalous or libellous reflections on the proceedings of the House and upon members individually have been considered as breaches of privilege.

Speech:
So my concern is not about a particular individual or group of individuals, it is about the system that we are establishing, the institutions that we are developing, and the way we are changing the nature of government in Canada.
As I said earlier, I agree with the motives of the Prime Minister in trying to establish around him as political head of the government what has been called, in the words of a former editor of Cite Libre, a countervailing force to the public service. But I make the point that there is in our system another countervailing force to the power of government, and it is this House of Commons. The danger is that a serious imbalance is growing between the power of the Prime Minister and the cabinet and the capacity to countervail that power in this House of Commons.
I raise these matters now because, despite the scope of the change that we have seen in the way we are governed here, this bill is unfortunately the only specific opportunity that we in this House have to discuss this very serious change in the nature of the government of Canada. That is to say, it is unless the Prime Minister, when he brings forward the changes in the rules that he is proposing-or perhaps I should say threatening-also proposes a means by which we, as an institution, can control those new
Federal-Provincial Relations
agencies that have grown up to create the imbalance between the power of the ministry and of this parliament.
I want to speak very briefly about those fellows and the very few women in the public service who earn so much more than do members of the House of Commons, namely, our senior public servants, particularly those who are appointed at the discretion of the Prime Minister and who do not have to go through the Public Service Commission. I repeat, I can understand and approve personally of the Prime Minister's desire, as political head of the government, to try to control and direct his own government and not let the job be done by senior public servants. But I think it would be wrong for us to ignore the fact that there has been in recent days, indeed years, reason for suspicion that appointments to senior positions have been for reasons other than merit. I suggest these reasons have also to do with loyalty, not necessarily loyalty to a party but loyalty to a point of view that might be embodied in a minister.
I think it would be a very real danger, particularly in a country of such diversity, and frankly such fragility, as Canada, if we developed, in effect, a personal public service at the senior level. The appointment of Mr. Pitfield clearly raises the fear, as do the consequent resignations- I use those words deliberately-of other senior deputy ministers in tandem, that we are developing a public service that is chosen not simply because of its competence but also because of its loyalty to the particular point of view that happens to occupy the treasury benches at the present time. That is a serious situation for our system of government to face.
There is one other aspect I want to touch on today and it relates also to parliament and our powers and prerogatives. It is very clear to me, and I think to many members on this side of the House, that the growth in formal relations and conferences between the federal government and the provincial governments, indeed the various levels of government, seriously threatens to undercut the authority and the role of the House of Commons. There is the inexorable danger that these new processes that we are developing will by-pass parliament and will mean that decisions are taken at some place other than this place; and it is this place where, under our system, decisions are supposed to be taken.
Reference was made earlier by my collegue from Edmonton-Strathcona to the discussions that took place at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary in the summer of 1973. At that time issues of great importance to western Canada were raised by the premiers, and commitments were given by various ministers. Many of those commitments have not been honoured, but that is not really the point. The point is that the demands made during those few days in Calgary by the premiers were demands that had been made time and time again, year after year after year, by members of the House of Commons. The difference was that in Calgary, in speaking to the premiers the ministers gave commitments; in the House of Commons, speaking to members of parliament, the representatives of those regions, the government was evasive or gave no answers at all.

Speech:
That is a very serious undermining of the power and prerogatives of this place. My colleague for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) calls it a contempt for parliament, and I think that is literally what it is. I do not think it is the purpose of ministers deliberately to tear down parliament, but I think this is what is happening. Over a period of time they have started to pay more attention and to attribute more seriousness to issues raised by premiers, in private or public conferences, than to representations made by the people who are elected to this House from those regions where these issues arise.
There is a danger that, by creating this special office we are speaking of today, we are going to contribute and add to that process of bringing down the authority of parliament, and making it easy for the government to by-pass this place which is, in theory and in fact, the most effective arena and institution to control a government given to excess.
The hon. member for Scarborough East spoke about complexities when he defended the establishment of a special office for federal-provincial relations. As I recall from sitting in the gallery at that time, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), when he had responsibility as House leader, spoke of the complexities which parliament and the government must face when he proposed the changes to the rules of this House. Whenever there is an attempt to downgrade or by-pass parliament the excuse is complexity, that events are coming on too fast and are too complicated for this Chamber to handle. That bespeaks the assumption that parliament cannot deal with complexity, and that assumption, so long as it is in the saddle, is literally fatal to this system.
That assumption ensures that we will continue to be undermined and that the powers of this institution will continue to go down. As I say, I think that is a danger in the institution we are establishing today, particularly since this new office will be answerable only to a prime minister who is not in any practical way answerable to this House of Commons.
I want to repeat what we all know, that we are not a federal system by accident, we are a federal system because we have to be. This is a highly diverse country which requires a government that is in tune with its diversities. It is certain to all of us, I think, that this parliament is the best representation of diversity, drawing as it does individuals from every locality in the land, and paying attention, as its tradition insists, to the rights of those individuals to speak on behalf of their localities. No other agency of government does this, and it cannot be guaranteed in the public service where people in order to become promoted to levels of effective decision making have to live here so long they forget where they came from, Mr. Speaker. This cannot be done either in private conferences, involving various premiers. It cannot be done with guarantees in any other but this forum.
The strength of parliament is not an academic thing at all. It is important to the very roots of this federal country. Every time we wear it down or by-pass parliament, and every time we set up agencies to deal with problems that

are too complex for parliament, we literally put federalism into danger, as well as damage the parliamentary system of government to which we claim allegiance.
My point in this intervention, which has gone on longer that I intended, is that there has been a range of serious changes in the way in which we have been governed in this country in the last ten years. Since I came here in 1972, and during the longer period when I was watching events from the gallery, this is the only time at which parliament itself has had the chance to pass judgment on the growth of power. The other powers have been developed without recourse to parliament, and without our having the opportunity to debate them and to express whatever concerns we had. What is remarkable about this bill is not that it has come before us, but that so many other bills which should have come before us did not. With so many of the powers of the Prime Minister and the executive being developed in this country without recourse to the House of Commons, this is a very serious situation.
I hope that when this bill reaches the committee we will be able to review not only the powers that will attach to this new official, not only his relation to the Prime Minister, but also we will be able to review the range of powers of people and agencies appointed by the executive, so that we can begin to achieve the balance which was written into this system when it began-a balance between the executive and elected representatives of this very diverse country.

Mr. Speaker, Customs Tariff ways and means bills are always interesting to look at, although I suspect there is generally not much interest in them from the public's point of view. In many ways they are outlines of changes in the government's policy and attitude. Customs Tariffs have been used since the beginning of Canadian history in this regard. Another feature of this bill is that it is loaded with all kinds of anomalies, as has been the case with bills of

January 22, 1975
Customs Tariff
this kind going back to confederation. One wonders why many items have continued to be subject to Customs Tariff for as long as they have. I have in mind two items that come in under the most favoured nation and Commonwealth preference. It may be that at some time in the 1800s someone in Canada was manufacturing cricket bats and the government decided to provide some protection, so cricket bats were made subject to tariff. This is now being changed and cricket bats will not be subject to any tariff provided they are brought in from a Commonwealth country.
Another item I have always been curious about is bananas. Why in the world we should have a tariff on bananas coming into Canada when, in fact, except under most extraordinary circumstances, we have no way of growing them here, is something that has escaped me. In attempting to get an answer to this question I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) why we continued to have a tariff on bananas. He replied that there is competition in respect of different kinds of foods, and if people eat bananas they will not eat tomatoes-and we grow tomatoes here. In any event, I am glad to see that the tariff is coming off bananas.
In the past, Customs Tariffs have been used as instruments of combines policy. The royal commission report in the 1950s suggested that companies which colluded with each other in forming a combine against the public interest should be penalized by having their tariff protection removed. Since then two major cases have occurred, one in respect of the glass industry and the other in respect of the fine papers industry. In neither of those cases was the tariff removed. The companies were permitted to continue in operation, having been found guilty of collusion.
The interesting thing about this bill is that it represents a definite change in government attitude. Apparently the government is no longer worrying so much about industry but is more concerned with protecting the consumer. It is fairly obvious that the proposed changes are designed to lower prices to the consumer. This is in contrast to previous Customs Tariff bills. Certainly, in many ways it is a departure from government policy. To a very large extent, the government has in the past taken the position that it would not change tariffs because it wished to use them as negotiating tools in order to obtain concessions from other countries. By this bill it would seem the government has dropped this negotiating tool approach in favour of attempting to assist consumers. Even in this regard we find inconsistencies which illustrate the conflict which exists in government policy.
As an example, let us consider the situation regarding mobile homes. On the one hand we find that the mobile home industry in Canada is being protected by tariff provisions. When the government proposed the removal of excise tax on building materials, the proposal did not apply to mobile homes. This results in the fact that mobile homes are protected on the one hand and disadvantaged on the other, with the result that from two directions those who have a preference for mobile homes are penalized by having to pay higher prices than would normally be the case. Mobile homes represent an important aspect of housing in Canada, and as such are deserving of consideration. This situation will have to be straightened out

by the government. The industry is penalized on the one hand and rewarded on the other.
I suspect there is not a great deal of opposition to this bill. It does indicate the direction of government policy. Specifically, it indicates the government's concern regarding certain agricultural products-beef, for example. The government intended to remove some of the tariffs on processed beef. There is still a substantial tariff in respect of sugar in spite of the fact that the sugar beet industry in Canada is not producing the volumes it once did when protection was required. It seems to me, the price of sugar being what it is, that the government might have removed the tariff on this commodity. I do not anticipate any difficulty in agreeing to the provisions of this bill.

First, may I say that I believe that all of us agree with the desire of the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), namely, that persons who have been in Canada for 3 years, have landed immigrant status, and desire to become Canadian citizens, should be able to do so within that period of time rather than having to wait as long as the law at present requires.
As both of the previous speakers have pointed out, there is a slight difference between the provision in Bill C-209 and the provision in this respect that is contained in Bill C-20. This, of course, can be sorted out in committee, and I think it is a good idea to have the proposal of a private member go to that committee along with the government bill.
Therefore we are happy to support the motion which, I presume, will be made at some point by way of an amendment that the subject matter of Bill C-20 be referred to the appropriate standing committee.
Canadian Citizenship Act
The suggestion I would like to make relates to a couple of bills of mine that are on the order paper. One of them is Bill C-260 and the other is Bill C-317. Both of these bills also relate to changes that I think should be made in the Citizenship Act, and I hope that the House might also be willing to allow the subject matter of these two bills to go to the same committee along with the subject matter of Bill C-209.
They are Orders Nos. 60 and 117, or Bills C-260 and C-317. Both of these bills are particularly appropriate in International Women's Year. The first one, Bill C-260, has to do with the citizenship of a child born outside of Canada. As the law now stands, such a child can, under certain conditions, become a Canadian citizen if the child is the child of a father who is a Canadian citizen. This is not permitted if it is only the mother who is a Canadian citizen, except in the case of an illegitimate child. Surely it is time to straighten that out, Mr. Speaker. I have the feeling that Bill C-20 takes care of it, but just to make sure that this point was covered I gave notice of my Bill C-260, and I hope that the subject matter of it might also be referred to the standing committee.
The other bill, Bill C-317, has to do with another discrimination against females. As the law now stands, if a Canadian male citizen brings in a wife who is not a Canadian, she can become a Canadian citizen in one year. In other words the male Canadian citizen can confer a certain right on his spouse. But if a female Canadian citizen brings in a husband who is not a Canadian citizen, he has to wait five years. In other words a Canadian male can confer a certain right on his spouse that is denied a Canadian female.

Speech:
Madam Speaker, because of the lateness of the hour I will cut short my opening remarks and simply say that the housing

January 29, 1975
National Housing Act
problem that we now have is not only a national problem but a very intense local problem in certain areas of the country, and also a very individual problem for certain segments of our population.
There is a group of people who, because of special needs, are attracted to special locations, specific areas in our country, and I refer of course to the special needs of our senior citizens. These are people who are hurt beyond the hurt of all other segments of the population in this critical area of housing. They are people who, because of transportation needs, must live near the urban areas, and this, coincidentally is also the area of greatest cost for housing. Frequently because of health they tend to move towards the areas of Canada where the climate is more moderate, such as southern Ontario, southern B.C., Surrey-White Rock, Greater Vancouver, and Greater Victoria. It is the very attractiveness of these areas that creates the congestion. The congestion accelerates the shortage, inflates the prices, and puts these facilities out of reach of tjie people who need them the most.
But the greatest problem is that we see it as a problem. There was a time when the elderly were counted as an asset; today they are counted as a problem. Their accumulated wisdom at one time in our history was seen as a source of wealth. Their well formed opinions were seen as a force for stability. Their scope of experience was seen as a comprehension which complemented our fixation on specialization. These we considered as assets. So long as we see senior citizens as a problem we will produce half hearted solutions that tantalize rather than cure. It is no solution to invent polite euphemisms such as golden age clubs, sunset pavilions, retirement centres. Euphemisms such as that are not a cure. One hundred years ago the English poet, Robert Browning, in a poem entitled "Rabbi Ben Ezra", said:
Grow old along with me The Best Is yet to come The last of life, for which the
first was made.
I wonder how many senior citizens in our country today would be able to say with Rabbi Ben Ezra "Grow old along with me, the best is yet to come" when they are presented with a housing problem such as we have never seen before.
We have a variety of programs today for senior citizens but, no matter how they are designed, the programs always seem to end up with a housing solution that pensioners cannot afford-the payments are beyond their income, and those elderly who are on fixed income are tantalized by senior citizens' programs that are beyond their reach.
So I would like to make one suggestion to the minister to help in something that might be at least a partial solution to them, and I refer specifically to programs for non-profit senior citizens projects. Those programs are already burdened with land acquisition costs, and the private citizens who have combined resources to help senior citizens in this way have already given extensively. Yet, beyond that there is the expense of the combination of federal and provincial mortgages. In truth, there are some grants given them, but these mortgage payments are at interest rates that they cannot afford. On top of that there are property taxes. Even if the mortgage payments were such that senior citizens could afford them, there are the property taxes which the municipalities cannot afford to forgo because they need this revenue, and the property taxes help to put those projects out of reach of senior citizens.
So I would like to propose to the minister that he consider a program whereby mortgage payments on nonprofit senior citizens housing projects would be forgiven to the level of 50 per cent of the property taxes. In this way the revenue which the municipalities need would be retained for those areas. This would focus on areas of our country where the pressure in housing is the greatest on senior citizens. It would tend to alleviate the pressure in those areas; it would focus on the areas where it is felt most by senior citizens, and it would help to alleviate the pressure on that segment of the population that can least afford this kind of regular housing.
I would invite the minister to consider this proposal to forgive 50 per cent of the mortgage payments on non-profit senior citizens housing projects to the level of 50 per cent of the property taxes. I trust that this will find favour with the minister.
May I call it six o'clock, Madam Speaker?

Madam Speaker, I should like to speak briefly about a specific aspect of the Income Tax Act. I refer to the much publicized $1,000 clause which supposedly permits a person to reduce his or her taxable income by $1,000 providing that person has earned at least $1,000 in interest from Canadian investments. As outlined in Item 35 in the 1974 income tax guide, a taxpayer's eligible interest must also first be reduced by the total of all interest deductions claimed in the computation of income from other sources reported on the return. This all sounds pretty good at first reading, but closer examination reveals some apparent shortcomings, and even discriminations.
First, it would appear that if an individual owns an apartment building and has a mortgage or bank loan against the property on which he is paying interest charges, then the interest charges must be offset against the exemption under the $1,000 interest earned allowance. If this is actually the case then I feel there are a number of reasons why the situation should be rectified.
The purpose of other main points in the budget was to encourage investment in rental accommodation and property. The above-mentioned situation would do the opposite. Furthermore, the purpose of the $1,000 exemption was to produce investment income, the net of which is taxable. I feel, therefore, that bank or mortgage interest paid in connection with the operation of a business should be considered as having to be deductions from the $1,000 exemption allowance.
Another apparent discrimination in this section of the Income Tax Act is that, in order for a married couple to receive any benefit of exemption on the wife's earnings, it would appear that she would have had to earn over $1,806 during the taxable year and, therefore, not be a deduction herself. This is, of course, when the husband has earned the bulk of the couple's income.
This appears to be a strong discrimination against the spouse of a taxpayer, and would in most cases be a discrimination against women. Because of the fact that many times it is the spouse who acquires the savings of a married couple, this loophole would be a sizeable detriment to investments. I call it a loophole because I am giving the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the benefit of the suggestion that this slip-up was inadvertent.
With the cost of living as high as it is, and rising at the unprecedented rate that it is, the low and middle income people of this country need all the tax relief available to help them make ends meet. This does not mean introducing a much ballyhooed tax exemption that is comprised of a bunch of promises and fine print. The intent of the legislation, meagre as it might be, has to be effectively met. To ensure this we must be certain that all Canadian taxpayers will be eligible to claim the full benefit of the $1,000 deduction. Therefore these discrepancies must be investigated and rectified.

After the budget, however, it gets 4.9 per cent. Who took what from whom? Who is doing what to whom?
The Minister of Finance talks about fair sharing between the federal government, the provincial governments and the industry. It is sophistry. It is chicanery. Any accountant, Mr. Speaker, would call a royalty a proper business expense. Any economist would call a royalty a proper business expense. Royalties have been allowed as a proper business expense since companies began paying corporation taxes.
Under this budget if a royalty is paid to a private mineral owner like the CPR or the Hudson Bay Company, it will be allowed as a business expense. If a royalty is paid to someone in Montana or Texas, it will be allowed as a proper business expense. But if a royalty is paid to the people of Saskatchewan, it will not be allowed as a proper business expense.
